newsitem.title: BELGIUM: WEU offers help in central Africa.
newsitem.headline: WEU offers help in central Africa.

text.p: Western European Union (WEU) foreign and defence ministers said on Tuesday they were willing to provide air and logistics support in a humanitarian aid effort in Africa's troubled Great Lakes region.

In a move hailed by France as a way for Europe to raise its profile on the international stage, the ministers said the 10-nation defence group would seek to reinforce efforts by the international community.
"It is not a matter of acting instead of others, but by their side," French European Affairs Minister Michel Barnier told reporters.

At a meeting in the Belgian seaside town of Ostend, the ministers said the WEU should study what help it could provide and would act if asked to do so by EU foreign ministers, who meet in Brussels next Monday.
The WEU, often described as the European Union's fledgling defence arm, links 10 EU members -- all but Austria, Denmark, Sweden, Ireland and Finland, whose ministers were attending as observers.
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel, who played down the move, said the kinds of tasks the WEU might perform in the Great Lakes region included providing transport and possible mine clearing.
"It goes without saying that we want to help with the refugees," he said.
The ministers also emphasised the need to help African nations handle their own crises.
"The OAU, the largest regional organisation in the world, must try to find African solutions to African problems," Kinkel said, referring to the Organisation for African Unity.
WEU Secretary General Jose Cutileiro is to attend a meeting in Stuttgart, Germany, on Thursday of countries contributing to the Canadian-led mission to eastern Zaire.

The force's mission, however, grows less clear by the day. The U.N. refugee agency estimates that about half a million Hutu refugees have flocked home peacefully since Friday, deciding to quit the war zone in the Goma area of rebel-held eastern Zaire.

Many countries, such as the United States, Britain and South Africa, were reluctant volunteers in the first place and have seized on the mass migration as a sign that the force should be radically reduced in size or even scrapped.
France's Barnier accepted that the situation had changed recently in the region, but said help was still needed.
"We are happy that the refugees are returning voluntarily, but the situation is not stable," he said.
France is keen for European nations to project themselves more on the world stage as part of the EU's plans to integrate its foreign policy.

The WEU has taken a more important role in this since NATO, the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, said with Washington's blessing that it was willing to lend troops and equipment to the WEU for peacekeeping and humanitarian efforts.
Barnier said the offer of help in Africa was an example of the kind of European mission governments had had in mind when they agreed the idea in Berlin last June.
